'''''Tara spinosa''''', commonly known as '''''tara''''' ([[Quechua language|Quechua]]),<ref>Diccionario Quechua - Español - Quechua, Academía Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Gobierno Regional Cusco, Cusco 2005 (Quechua-Spanish dictionary)</ref> also known as '''Peruvian carob'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=2011-07-25|title=Market Survey - Tara|url=http://www.biocomercioperu.org/admin/recursos/contenidos/LdA%201%20-%20Estudio%20de%20Mercado%20tara.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110725073854/http://www.biocomercioperu.org/admin/recursos/contenidos/LdA%201%20-%20Estudio%20de%20Mercado%20tara.pdf|archive-date=2011-07-25|access-date=2021-07-08|website=Biocomercio Peru}}</ref> or '''spiny holdback''',<ref name=":0" /> is a small [[Legume|leguminous]] tree or thorny [[shrub]] native to [[Peru]].<ref>All information in article taken from: A. Brack Egg (1999). ''Diccionario Enciclopédico de Plantas Utiles del Perú'' Cusco, Peru: CBC.</ref> ''T. spinosa'' is cultivated as a source of [[tannin]]s based on a [[galloyl]]ated [[quinic acid]] structure.<ref>[http://www.fpl.fs.fed.us/documnts/pdf1997/galve97a.pdf Analytical Studies on Tara Tannins. J.M. Garro Galvez, B. Riedl and A. H. Conner, Holzforschung, 51(1997) 235-243] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110928055745/http://www.fpl.fs.fed.us/documnts/pdf1997/galve97a.pdf |date=2011-09-28 }}.</ref> This chemical structure has been confirmed also by [[Liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry|LC–MS]].<ref name = Clifford >M. N. Clifford, S. Stoupi and N. Kuhnert. [http://www.aseanfood.info/Articles/11021914.pdf ''Profiling and Characterization by LC-MSn of the Galloylquinic Acids of Green Tea, Tara Tannin, and Tannic Acid'']. J. Agric. Food Chem., 2007, 55 (8), pp. 2797-2807. DOI: 10.1021/jf063533l. Publication Date (Web): March 24, 2007.</ref> It is also grown as an [[ornamental plant]] because of its large colorful flowers and pods.

==Names and taxonomy==
Its common names include spiny holdback, ''tara'', ''taya'', and ''algarroba tanino'' (Peru).

''Tara spinosa'' is placed in the family [[Fabaceae]], subfamily [[Caesalpinioideae]], and tribe [[Caesalpinieae]].<ref>{{GRIN | accessdate = 17 December 2017}}</ref>

==Description==
''Tara spinosa'' typically grows {{Cvt|2-5|m|ft}} tall; its bark is dark gray with scattered prickles and hairy twigs. Leaves are alternate, evergreen, lacking [[stipule]]s, [[bipinnate]], and lacking petiolar and [[rachis]] glands. Leaves consist of three to ten pairs of primary [[leaflet (botany)|leaflets]] under {{Cvt|8|cm|}} in length, and five to seven pairs of subsessile elliptic secondary leaflets, each about {{Cvt|1.5-4|cm||sigfig=1}} long. [[Inflorescence]]s are {{Cvt|15-20|cm|}} long terminal [[raceme]]s, many flowered and covered in tiny hairs. Flowers are yellow to orange with 6- to 7-mm [[petal]]s; the lowest [[sepal]] is boat-shaped with many long marginal teeth; [[stamen]]s are yellow, irregular in length and barely protruding. The fruit is a flat, oblong [[indehiscent]] [[Legume|pod]], about {{Cvt|6-12|cm|}} long and {{Cvt|2.5|cm|}} wide, containing four to seven round black seeds, which redden when mature.<ref>E. McClintock (1996). Caesalpinia. ''In'': J.C. Hickman (ed.) The Jepson Manual: Higher Plants of California. University of California Press.</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Tara spinosa'' is native to Peru and can be found growing throughout northern, western, and southern South America, from Venezuela to Argentina. It has been introduced in drier parts of Asia, the Middle East, and Africa and has become naturalized in California. ''T. spinosa'' grows in the nearly rainless [[lomas]] or fog oases of the Peruvian coastal desert.<ref>Zaro, Gregory (2007), "Diversity Specialists: Coastal Resource Management and Historical Contingency in the Osmore Desert of Southern Peru," ''Latin American Antiquity'', Vol. 18, No. 2, pp. 165–174</ref>

Generally resistant to most pathogens and pests, it grows at elevations between 0 and {{Cvt|3000|m|}} above sea level, and tolerates dry climates and poor soils, including those high in sand and rocks. To propagate, seeds must be scarified (treated to break physical dormancy), and young plants should be transplanted to the field at {{Cvt|40|cm|}} in height; trees begin to produce after 4–5 years. Mature pods are usually harvested by hand and typically sun dried before processing. If well irrigated, trees can continue to produce for another 80 years, though their highest production is between 15 and 65 years of age.<ref>P. De la Cruz Lapa (2004). An integral and rational utility of tara (''Caesalpinia spinosa''-''Caesalpinia tinctoria'') Rev. Inst. investig. Fac. minas metal cienc. geogr. [online]. jul./dic. 2004, vol.7, no.14 [citado 27 Mayo 2008], p.64-73. <{{cite web |url=http://www.scielo.org.pe/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S1561-08882004000200009&lng=es&nrm=iso |title=Revista del Instituto de Investigación de la Facultad de Ingeniería Geológica, Minera, Metalurgica y Geográfica - '''Aprovechamiento integral y racional de la tara ''Caesalpinia spinosa - caesalpinia tinctoria''''' |accessdate=2008-05-27 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110722002645/http://www.scielo.org.pe/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S1561-08882004000200009&lng=es&nrm=iso |archivedate=2011-07-22 }}>.</ref>

==Uses==
===Industrial===
''Tara spinosa'' pods are an excellent source of [[tannin]]s (tara tannins) most commonly used in the manufacture of automotive and furniture leathers.<ref name = Escuer >J. C. Castell Escuer [http://www.tdx.cat/bitstream/handle/10803/81122/TJCE1de1.pdf?sequence=1 ''TARA (Caesalpinia spinosa): the sustainable source of tannins for innovative tanning processes'']. Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya (UPC). Barcelona, January 2012.</ref> This growing industry is developing around their production in Peru. Some producers have their own plantations to guarantee constant quality.

Tara tannin derivatives are being proposed as [[anti-fouling paint|antifouling]] against marine organisms that can grow on ship hulls.<ref name = Bellotti >N. Bellotti, B. Del Amo, R. Romagnoli. [http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211812812000363 ''Caesalpinia spinosa tannin derivatives for antifouling formulations'']. Procedia Materials Science, Volume 1, 2012, pp. 259-265. 11th International Congress on Metallurgy & Materials SAM/CONAMET 2011.</ref> Those tannins are of the [[hydrolysable tannin|hydrolysable type]]. [[Gallic acid]] is the main constituent of tara tannins (53%) and can be easily isolated by alkaline [[hydrolysis]] of the plant extract.<ref>J.M. Garro Galvez, B. Riedl and A. H. Conner (1997). Analytical Studies on Tara Tannins. Holzforschung 51: 235-243.</ref>

[[Quinic acid]] is also a constituent of the tara tannins.<ref name = Giovando >S. Giovando, A. Pizzi, H. Pasch and N. Pretorius. [http://www.proligno.ro/en/articles/2013/1/pizzi_full.pdf ''Structure and Oligomers Distribution of Commercial Tara (Caesalpina spinosa) Hydrolysable Tannin'']. PRO LIGNO Vol. 9 N° 1 2013, pp. 22-31, ISSN-L 1841-4737, ONLINE ISSN 2069-7430.</ref> Its tannins are colourless or light making them suitable a [[mordant|premordant]] in the [[dyeing]] of cotton and other cellulose fibres.<ref>[http://www.turkeyredjournal.com/archives/V19_I1/brown.html ''Donna Brown, Diane de Souza, and Catharine Ellis: Mordanting Cotton and Cellulose—Successful Methods, Turkey Red Journal 19:1 (2014)''].</ref>

The tree can also be a source of lumber and firewood, and as a live fence.{{Source needed|date=June 2025}}

The seeds can be used to produce black dye, while dark blue dye can be obtained from the roots.{{Source needed|date=June 2025}}

===Food additives===
Major food additives derived from ''T. spinosa'' include tara flour, which is potentially toxic, and tara gum, commonly used as a thickener and stabilizer.<ref name=fdamemo2024>{{cite letter|url=https://www.fda.gov/media/178582/download?attachment|author=FDA Toxicologist (Redacted)|recipient=Acting Director of Office of Food Additive Safety and Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition (Redacted)|date=10 April 2024|subject=Regulatory status and review of available information pertaining to tara protein/flour derived from the seed germ of the plant, ''Caesalpinia spinosa'': lack of general recognition of safety for its use in foods.|access-date=17 June 2024|publisher=U.S. Food & Drug Administration}}</ref>  Tara flour is produced from the germ (embryo) of the tara seed,<ref name=fdamemo2024/> while gum is produced from the seed's [[endosperm]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Maier|first1=Helmut|last2=Anderson|first2=Mark|last3=Karl|first3=Curt|last4=Magnuson|first4=Kenneth|last5=Whistler|first5=Roy L.|chapter=CHAPTER 8 - GUAR, LOCUST BEAN, TARA, AND FENUGREEK GUMS|title=Industrial Gums: Polysaccharides and Their Derivatives|edition=Third|editor-last1=Whistler|editor-first1=Roy L.|editor-last2=Bemiller|editor-first2=James N.|publisher=Academic Press|year=1993|isbn=0-12-746253-8|pages=181–226|doi=10.1016/B978-0-08-092654-4.50012-7}}</ref>

==== Tara flour toxicity in humans ====
At least 393 people who had consumed [[Daily Harvest|Daily Harvest’s]] "French Lentil and Leek Crumbles” in April-June 2022 became ill with signs of gastrointestinal disease and hepatotoxicity. <ref name=":1">{{Citation |title=Tara Flour |date=2012 |work=LiverTox: Clinical and Research Information on Drug-Induced Liver Injury |url=http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK604845/ |access-date=2026-07-12 |place=Bethesda (MD) |publisher=National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases |pmid=38985927}}</ref> Signs of toxicity occurred within 4-12 hours after ingestion and included abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. In some people clinical signs were severe enough to result in visits to the emergency department and hospitalisation with [[cholecystectomy]] performed.<ref name=":1" />  

On July 19, 2022, the food company [[Daily Harvest]] had identified tara flour, which is derived from the seeds of ''Tara spinosa'',<ref>{{Cite web | url = https://www.consumerreports.org/health/food-safety/skip-eating-products-that-contain-tara-flour-a5736602330/ | title = For Now, Skip Eating Products That Contain Tara Flour, CR's Food Experts Say | date = 22 July 2022 | publisher = Consumer Reports }}</ref> as the ingredient that had sickened hundreds of its customers.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Demetrakakes |first1=Pan |title=Regulatory Compliance - Tara Flour Behind Mysterious Illness |url=https://www.foodprocessing.com/industrynews/2022/tara-flour-behind-mysterious-illness/ |access-date=20 July 2022 |work=Food Processing |publisher=Endeavor Business Media |date=20 July 2022}}</ref> The manufacturer  removed the product from the market in June 2022 and no more cases were identified. 

Further analysis found [[Daily Harvest|Daily Harvest’s]] "French Lentil and Leek Crumbles” was free of contamination with known toxic compounds including microbial or viral pathogens, mycotoxins, allergens, heavy metals, and pesticides. However, one of the major ingredients was tara flour which contained several suspect non-protein amino acids including [[baikiain]] at 3% dry weight. Subsequent rodent studies showed [[baikiain]] as a liver toxin and is hypothesized to be the chemical compound responsible for the hepatotoxicity. <ref name=":1" /><ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1021/acs.chemrestox.3c00100 | title = Is Baikiain in Tara Flour a Causative Agent for the Adverse Events Associated with the Recalled Frozen French Lentil & Leek Crumbles Food Product? - A Working Hypothesis | year = 2023 | last1 = Chittiboyina | first1 = Amar G. | last2 = Ali | first2 = Zulfiqar | last3 = Avula | first3 = Bharathi | last4 = Khan | first4 = Shabana I. | last5 = Mir | first5 = Tahir M. | last6 = Zhang | first6 = Jin | last7 = Aydoğan | first7 = Fadime | last8 = Zulfiqar | first8 = Fazila | last9 = Techen | first9 = Natascha | last10 = Parveen | first10 = Iffat | last11 = Pandey | first11 = Pankaj | last12 = Adams | first12 = Sebastian J. | last13 = Wang | first13 = Yan-Hong | last14 = Zhao | first14 = Jianping | last15 = Marshall | first15 = Gailen D. | last16 = Pugh | first16 = Nirmal D. | last17 = Khan | first17 = Ikhlas A. | journal = Chemical Research in Toxicology | volume = 36 | issue = 6 | pages = 818–821 | pmid = 37255213 | s2cid = 258988288 | pmc = 10283043 }}</ref> 

A handful of lawsuits have been filed against the company.<ref name="STimes-tara">{{cite news |last1=Cornwell |first1=Paige |title=WA lawyer leads lawsuits in outbreak linked to Daily Harvest crumbles |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/wa-lawyer-leads-lawsuits-in-outbreak-linked-to-daily-harvest-crumbles/ |access-date=28 November 2022 |publisher=The Seattle Times |date=28 Nov 2022}}</ref>  

====Tara flour banned by FDA====
On May 15, 2024, the U.S. [[Food and Drug Administration|Food and Drug Administration (FDA)]] banned the use of tara flour, having determined tara flour in human food does not meet the [[generally recognized as safe]] (or GRAS) standard and is an unapproved food additive.<ref name="FDA-tara">{{Cite web | url = https://www.fda.gov/food/cfsan-constituent-updates/fda-update-post-market-assessment-tara-flour/ | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20240517195447/https://www.fda.gov/food/cfsan-constituent-updates/fda-update-post-market-assessment-tara-flour | url-status = dead | archive-date = May 17, 2024 | title = FDA Update on the Post-market Assessment of Tara Flour
 | date = 15 May 2024 | publisher = US Food and Drug Administration |access-date=18 May 2024 }}</ref><ref name="FC-tara">{{cite news |last1=Alsever |first1=Jennifer |title=The FDA finally rules that toxic tara flour once used by Daily Harvest is not safe to eat |url=https://www.fastcompany.com/91127185/tara-flour-toxic-fda-finding-daily-harvest-gras-loophole |access-date=18 May 2024 |publisher=Fast Company |date=18 May 2024}}</ref> 

====Tara gum====
Tara gum, produced from a different part of the tara seed, remains safe to consume. According to the FDA, tara gum has a well established safety profile and is "distinct from tara flour".<ref name="FDA-tara"></ref>
Tara [[Natural gum|gum]] is a white or beige, nearly odorless powder that is produced by separating and grinding the endosperm of ''T. spinosa'' seeds.<ref name=":0" /> Tara gum consists of a linear main chain of (1-4)-β-D-mannopyranose units attached by (1–6) linkages with [[α-D-galactopyranose]] units.<ref name = JECFA >[http://www.fao.org/ag/agn/jecfa-additives/specs/Monograph1/Additive-455.pdf ''TARA GUM''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070125133701/http://www.fao.org/ag/agn/jecfa-additives/specs/Monograph1/Additive-455.pdf |date=2007-01-25 }}. Prepared at the 30th JECFA (1986), published in FNP 37 (1986) and in FNP 52 (1992). Metals and arsenic specifications revised at the 57th JECFA (2001).</ref> The major component of the gum is a [[galactomannan]] [[polymer]] similar to the main components of [[guar]] and [[Carob|locust bean]] gums that are used widely in the food industry. The ratio of mannose to galactose in tara gum is 3:1.<ref name = Sittikijyothin >W. Sittikijyothin, D. Torres, M.P. Gonçalves. [http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0144861704003716 ''Modelling the rheological behaviour of galactomannan aqueous solutions'']. Carbohydrate Polymers, Volume 59, Issue 3, pp 339–350, 18 February 2005.</ref> Tara gum has been deemed safe for human consumption as a food additive.<ref>J.F. Borzelleca, B.N. Ladu, F.R. Senti, and J.L. Egle, Jr. (1993). Evaluation of the Safety of Tara Gum as a Food Ingredient: A Review of the Literature. Journal of the American College of Toxicology 12: 81–89.</ref>

Tara gum is used as a [[thickening agent]] and stabilizer in a number of food applications. A solution of tara gum is less viscous than a [[guar gum]] solution of the same concentration, but more viscous than a solution of [[locust bean gum]]. Furthermore, tara gum shows an intermediate acid stability between locust bean gum and guar gum. It resists the depolymerisation effect of organic acids down to a pH of 3.5. This gum is also stable to high-temperature treatment, up to 145 °C in a continuous process plant. Blends of tara with modified and unmodified starches can be produced which have enhanced stabilization and emulsification properties, and these are used in the preparation of convenience foods, such as [[ice cream]]. One example is the American ice cream brand [[Breyers]].{{Source needed|date=June 2025}}

The [[E number|European food additive number]] for tara gum is E417. Tara gum is listed on the Canadian List of Permitted Emulsifying, Gelling, Stabilizing or Thickening Agents (Lists of Permitted Food Additives) as item T.2B.<ref>{{cite web |title=List of Permitted Emulsifying, Gelling, Stabilizing or Thickening Agents (Lists of Permitted Food Additives) |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/food-nutrition/food-safety/food-additives/lists-permitted/4-emulsifying-gelling-stabilizing-thickening-agents.html |accessdate=10 July 2019|date=2006-11-27 }}</ref>
